category.name: Frontend
category.description: HTML semantics and forms, CSS layout and preprocessors, and modern JavaScript.

questions.text: Which CSS property changes the text color of an element?
questions.explanation: color sets the foreground (text) color and is inherited by descendants. font-color and text-color look plausible but are not CSS properties, so browsers ignore them.

questions.text: Which selector matches every <p> anywhere inside an element with class article, including deeply nested ones?
questions.explanation: The space is the descendant combinator, matching <p> at any depth inside .article. > matches only direct children, and p .article reverses the relationship.

questions.text: Which display value makes an element start on a new line and respect width and height?
questions.explanation: A block box starts on a new line and accepts width and height. inline-block also accepts dimensions but flows within a line, and contents removes the element's own box entirely.

questions.text: What does box-sizing: border-box; change?
options: Margin is included in the element's declared width and height
Padding is excluded from the element's declared width and height
Padding and border are included in the element's declared width and height
The element always stretches to 100% of its parent's width
questions.explanation: With border-box, the declared width covers content, padding and border, so the content area shrinks to fit. Margins always remain outside the box.

questions.text:
What is the rendered border-box width of this element?

.card {
  box-sizing: content-box;
  width: 320px;
  padding: 24px;
  border: 2px solid #64748b;
  margin: 16px;
}
questions.explanation: Under content-box, width sizes only the content: 320 + 2×24 padding + 2×2 border = 372px. Margins add space outside the border, so they are not part of the border-box width.

questions.text: Which pseudo-class applies a style while the pointer is over an element?
questions.explanation: :hover matches while the pointer rests on the element. :active matches while it is being pressed, and :focus when it has focus, so don't rely on hover alone for interactions keyboard users need.

questions.text: What does margin: 10px 20px; set?
options: Top and bottom to 10px, left and right to 20px
Left and right to 10px, top and bottom to 20px
Top to 10px and right to 20px, leaving the others at 0
All four sides to the average value of 15px
questions.explanation: With two values, the first sets top and bottom and the second sets left and right. Four values go clockwise: top, right, bottom, left.

questions.text: Which declarations create a layout with two equal-width columns?
questions.explanation: Grid track properties only work on a grid container, and 1fr 1fr splits the free space into two equal columns. grid-columns and flex-columns are not CSS properties.

questions.text: How do you make text bold using CSS?
questions.explanation: font-weight controls boldness (bold equals 700). font-style handles italics and font-variant handles small caps, so neither accepts bold.

questions.text: Which unit is relative to the root element's font size?
questions.explanation: rem ("root em") is based on the <html> element's font size, so it stays consistent at any nesting depth. em is relative to the current element's font size and compounds when nested.

questions.text:
What is the child's computed padding?

html   { font-size: 16px; }
.parent { font-size: 20px; }
.child  { font-size: 1.5em; padding: 1em; }
questions.explanation: The child's font size is 1.5 × 20px = 30px. For other properties such as padding, em refers to the element's own computed font size, so 1em is 30px.

questions.text: What is the initial value of the position property?
questions.explanation: Elements are position: static by default and follow normal flow, so top, left and z-index have no effect. relative must be set explicitly.

questions.text: Which property controls the space between lines of text?
questions.explanation: line-height sets the height of each line box; unitless values such as 1.5 scale with the font size. letter-spacing and word-spacing adjust horizontal spacing.

questions.text: Which media query matches viewports narrower than 600px, but not exactly 600px?
questions.explanation: Range syntax width < 600px excludes 600px and is supported in all modern browsers. max-width: 600px is equivalent to width <= 600px, so it still matches at exactly 600px.

questions.text: Which property adds space between an element's content and its border?
questions.explanation: Padding sits inside the border and shows the element's background. Margin is outside the border, and border-spacing only applies to table cells.

questions.text: Which declaration rounds the corners of a square element into a full circle?
questions.explanation: A 50% radius on each corner of a square meets in the middle of each side, producing a circle. shape-outside only changes how text wraps around a float, and outline-radius is not a standard property.

questions.text: Which pseudo-element, written in standard syntax, inserts generated content before an element's content?
questions.explanation: ::before (with the content property) creates a first child box. The double colon marks pseudo-elements; browsers also accept legacy :before. :first-child is a pseudo-class that selects an existing element.

questions.text: How do you let flex items wrap onto multiple lines?
questions.explanation: flex-wrap: wrap lets items move to new lines when they run out of space; the default nowrap keeps them on one line and may shrink or overflow them. flex-direction only accepts row or column values.

questions.text: Which property makes an element semi-transparent, including its children?
questions.explanation: opacity takes 0–1 and applies to the element and all its contents. visibility: hidden hides the element completely while keeping its space, and transparency is not a CSS property.

questions.text: How do you define a global CSS custom property?
questions.explanation: Custom properties are declared like ordinary properties with a -- prefix, usually on :root so every element inherits them, and read with var(--main-color). $main-color is Sass syntax.

questions.text: Which property controls whether a background image tiles?
questions.explanation: background-repeat accepts values such as repeat, no-repeat, repeat-x and space. background-position sets where the image starts, and background-size sets how large it is.

questions.text: What does justify-content: space-between; do in a flex container?
options: Centers all items along the cross axis
Packs all items at the start of the main axis
Puts the first item at the start, the last at the end, and spaces the rest evenly
Stretches items so they fill the main axis
questions.explanation: space-between distributes free space only between items, with none before the first or after the last. space-around and space-evenly also add space at the edges.

questions.text: In a flex container with flex-direction: row, which declaration centers items vertically?
questions.explanation: In a row, the cross axis is vertical, and align-items aligns items on the cross axis. justify-content works on the main (horizontal) axis, and vertical-align doesn't apply to flex items.

questions.text: A flex container has flex-direction: column. Along which direction does justify-content now distribute items?
options: Horizontally, because justify-content always uses the inline axis
Vertically, because the main axis now runs top to bottom
Neither, because justify-content is ignored in column layouts
Diagonally, because both axes are swapped
questions.explanation: justify-content always acts on the main axis, and flex-direction: column makes the main axis vertical. align-items then works horizontally.

questions.text: In Flexbox, which declaration makes items fill the container's cross axis (and is the default)?
questions.explanation: align-items: stretch is the initial value, so items without a fixed cross size fill the line's height in a row. flex-grow distributes extra space along the main axis instead.

questions.text: Which selector has the highest specificity?
questions.explanation: It scores (1,2,1): one ID, two classes, one type. body div#container .item span is (1,1,3). After an equal ID count, the class column decides, so the number of type selectors doesn't matter.

questions.text:
What color is the paragraph?

<p class="b a">Hello</p>

.a { color: red; }
.b { color: blue; }
options: Red, because a is listed last in the class attribute
Blue, because .b comes later in the stylesheet
Red, because .a comes first in the stylesheet
Purple, because the two colors are mixed
questions.explanation: Both selectors have equal specificity (0,1,0), so source order decides and the later rule wins. The order of names in the class attribute has no effect on the cascade.

questions.text: What does !important do to a declaration?
options: Lowers the specificity of the rule
Makes it beat normal declarations, regardless of their selector specificity
Delays it until all other rules have been applied
Converts the rule into an inline style
questions.explanation: Important declarations take precedence over normal ones in the cascade, so specificity only matters between two declarations that are both important. Use it sparingly; it makes later overrides hard.

questions.text:
What color is the link?

<nav class="nav"><a class="btn" href="/">Home</a></nav>

@layer base, components;

@layer components {
  .btn { color: blue; }
}

@layer base {
  .nav .btn { color: red; }
}
options: Blue, because components is listed later in the @layer statement
Red, because the base block appears last in the file
The browser default, because conflicting layers cancel out
questions.explanation: For normal declarations, layer order is checked before specificity, and the first @layer base, components; statement fixes that order. A later layer wins even with a less specific selector.

questions.text: In CSS Grid, what does grid-template-areas let you do?
options: Generate grid tracks automatically from the content
Name regions and place items with an ASCII-art layout
Define the breakpoints at which the grid changes
Control the stacking order of overlapping grid items
questions.explanation: You draw rows of named cells as strings, such as "header header" "sidebar main", then put an item into a region with grid-area: main.

questions.text: Which CSS function is designed for fluid font sizes with a minimum and a maximum?
questions.explanation: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem) uses the preferred middle value but never goes below the minimum or above the maximum. min() or max() alone only enforce one bound.

questions.text: How do you write a container query that applies when the container is at least 400px wide?
questions.explanation: @container queries the nearest ancestor that is a size container. container-type is the property that creates that container, not an at-rule.

questions.text: A component's @container (min-width: 30rem) { … } rules never apply, although its wrapper is 40rem wide. What is the most likely cause?
options: Container queries only accept pixel units, not rem
The wrapper needs display: grid to act as a container
The rules must be repeated inside a matching @media query
questions.explanation: An element is only queried as a size container when it sets container-type, so without it the query finds no container. Any display type and length unit works.

questions.text: Which pseudo-class matches a focused element only when the browser decides focus should be visibly indicated, typically after keyboard navigation?
questions.explanation: :focus-visible uses browser heuristics: keyboard focus usually matches, while a mouse click on a button usually doesn't. :focus matches any focus, and :focus-within matches ancestors of the focused element.

questions.text: What does contain: layout paint; do?
options: Prevents child elements from inheriting styles
Isolates the element's layout and painting from the rest of the page
Disables pointer events inside the element
Hides the element until all its images have loaded
questions.explanation: Containment tells the browser that changes inside the element can't affect layout outside it and that its contents are clipped to its box, so less of the page needs recalculating or repainting.

questions.text: Which declaration, on its own, creates a new stacking context?
questions.explanation: Any transform other than none creates a stacking context. opacity only does so when below 1, and positioned elements need a z-index other than auto.

questions.text: How do you read a custom property with a fallback value?
questions.explanation: The first argument of var() is the property name, and anything after the first comma is the fallback used when the property is not defined.

questions.text: Which selector matches elements with class a or b while adding zero specificity?
questions.explanation: :where() always has specificity 0, so it is easy to override. :is() and :not() take the specificity of their most specific argument, and a plain list keeps each class at (0,1,0).

questions.text: What does will-change: transform; tell the browser?
options: To skip the element during painting
That transform is about to change, so it can prepare optimizations in advance
To remove the element from the layout flow
To polyfill transforms in older browsers
questions.explanation: It is a hint that lets the browser, for example, promote the element to its own layer before an animation starts. Overusing it wastes memory, so apply it only to elements that will actually animate.

questions.text: Which pair of properties can usually be animated without triggering layout recalculation?
questions.explanation: Browsers can apply transform and opacity changes during compositing without reflowing the page. Animating size, offsets or spacing forces layout on every frame and can cause jank and layout shifts.

questions.text: Which CSS function performs arithmetic with mixed units, such as 100% - 2rem?
questions.explanation: calc() is resolved by the browser, so it can combine units like % and rem that a preprocessor can't know at build time. expression() was an old, non-standard Internet Explorer feature.

questions.text: How does a nested grid item reuse the column tracks of its parent grid?
questions.explanation: The child must itself be a grid, and setting subgrid as its column template makes it use the parent's column lines, so nested content stays aligned. inherit only copies the parent's track list.

questions.text: Which media feature detects that the user prefers a dark color scheme?
questions.explanation: prefers-color-scheme reflects the operating-system or browser setting. color-scheme is a property that tells the browser which schemes a page supports, not a media feature.

questions.text: Which at-rule limits styles to a DOM subtree, optionally stopping at an inner boundary?
questions.explanation: @scope applies its rules only inside the scoping root and excludes anything inside the to (…) limit. @layer changes cascade priority and @container queries container size; neither limits which elements match.

questions.text: Which declaration makes in-page anchor links scroll smoothly instead of jumping?
questions.explanation: scroll-behavior on the scrolling container controls navigation and programmatic scrolls. Wrap it in prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference for users who reduce motion, as Bootstrap's Reboot does.

questions.text:
In native CSS nesting (and Sass), what does this rule match?

.card {
  &.featured { border-color: gold; }
}
options: An element that has both the card and featured classes
A .featured element that directly follows a .card
questions.explanation: & stands for the parent selector, and writing &.featured with no space produces .card.featured, the same element. & .featured, with a space, would match a descendant.

questions.text: Why can setting --accent on .card[data-tone="warning"] recolor a card in the browser, while changing a Sass $accent cannot?
options: Sass variables only work inside media queries
Sass variables are replaced with values at compile time; custom properties cascade at runtime
Custom properties are faster because they skip the cascade
Sass variables are scoped to the :root element only
questions.explanation: Compiled CSS contains only the value of $accent, not the variable. A custom property remains in the CSS, so an attribute or class on an element can override it through the cascade.

questions.text: In SCSS, how do you declare a variable?
questions.explanation: Sass variables start with $. @primary-color is Less syntax, and %name is a Sass placeholder selector, not a variable.

questions.text: In modern Dart Sass, which rule loads another Sass file as a module whose members are accessed through a namespace?
questions.explanation: @use loads a module once and exposes its members as buttons.$var or buttons.mixin(). @import puts everything in a global namespace and is deprecated, while @forward re-exports members for other files.

questions.text: In Sass, what does @forward 'src/list'; do?
options: Copies the file's CSS output without exposing its members
Makes the file's members available to stylesheets that @use the current file
Loads the file and lets the current file use its members directly
Removes unused selectors from the file
questions.explanation: @forward re-exports a module's variables, mixins and functions, which is how an index file builds a library's public API. It does not make those members available in the forwarding file itself; that needs @use.

questions.text: How do you define a mixin named button in SCSS?
questions.explanation: @mixin defines a reusable block of declarations. @function defines something that returns a value, %button is a placeholder selector, and @include uses a mixin rather than defining one.

questions.text: How do you include a Sass mixin called button?
questions.explanation: @include copies the mixin's declarations into the current rule and can pass arguments, as in @include button(red). @extend shares selectors instead of copying declarations.

questions.text:
What does @content do inside this Sass mixin?

@mixin small-viewport {
  @media (max-width: 30em) {
    @content;
  }
}

.nav {
  @include small-viewport {
    flex-direction: column;
  }
}
options: Outputs the mixin's own default styles
Inserts the block passed to @include at that position
Includes the contents of a file named content
Marks where the media query's breakpoint value goes
questions.explanation: A block written after @include is passed to the mixin and placed where @content appears, so the output is @media (max-width: 30em) { .nav { flex-direction: column; } }.

questions.text: Which Sass selector shares styles through @extend but is never output on its own?
questions.explanation: Placeholder selectors (%name) are only emitted when another selector extends them, so no unused class appears in the CSS. A .shared class would be output even if nothing uses it.

questions.text: How do you make a Sass selector inherit the styles of .btn?
questions.explanation: @extend .btn; adds the current selector to every rule that targets .btn. @include only works with mixins, not with selectors.

questions.text: Which Sass control rule loops over each item in a list or map?
questions.explanation: @each $color in red, green, blue { … } runs once per item, and it can also destructure map key/value pairs. @for counts through a numeric range instead.

questions.text:
Which classes does this Sass loop generate?

@for $i from 1 to 3 {
  .item-#{$i} { width: 100px * $i; }
}
questions.explanation: to excludes the end value, so $i takes 1 and 2. Use through to include 3.

questions.text: With @use 'sass:map';, which call returns the value stored under a key in a map?
questions.explanation: map.get is the module-system name for the legacy global map-get(), which is deprecated. Sass has no bracket indexing for maps.

questions.text: With @use 'sass:map';, how do you merge two maps?
questions.explanation: map.merge returns a new map in which keys from $map2 override matching keys in $map1. Using + on maps is an error because maps aren't valid CSS values.

questions.text: In current Dart Sass, which call darkens $c by 20% lightness without using a deprecated function?
questions.explanation: The legacy global darken() still compiles but triggers deprecation warnings. The sass:color module has no darken, and its replacement is color.adjust (or color.scale for relative changes).

questions.text: In current Dart Sass, which expression is the recommended way to divide 10px by 2?
questions.explanation: After @use 'sass:math';, math.div() performs division explicitly. Using / for division is deprecated because / is also a CSS separator, as in font: 16px/1.5.

questions.text: How do you nest a .card rule inside .container in SCSS?
questions.explanation: A rule nested inside another compiles to a descendant selector: .container .card { … }. Reversing the nesting would produce .card .container.

questions.text: How do you declare a variable in Less?
questions.explanation: Less variables use @ and are replaced at compile time. $ is Sass syntax, and --primary-color declares a native CSS custom property that the browser resolves.

questions.text: How do you import another Less file?
questions.explanation: Less uses @import to pull in other files, and the .less extension can be omitted. Unlike Sass, Less has no @use module system.

questions.text:
What does this Less code define?

.border(@width: 1px) {
  border: @width solid;
}
options: A parametric mixin with a default argument, not output as a class on its own
A variable named .border that stores 1px solid
A function that returns the value 1px
A .border class that is always written to the CSS output
questions.explanation: Parentheses in the definition make it a parametric mixin. It is only output where it is called, as .border(); or .border(2px);.

questions.text: How do you call a mixin named .center() in Less?
questions.explanation: Less mixins are called by writing the mixin's selector followed by (); inside a rule. @include is Sass syntax.

questions.text:
What does this Less guard do?

.rounded(@radius) when (@radius > 0) {
  border-radius: @radius;
}
options: Applies the mixin on every call, whatever the value
Applies the mixin only when @radius is greater than 0
Applies the mixin only when @radius is less than 0
Raises a compile error when @radius is 0
questions.explanation: A when guard is a condition on the mixin. If it is false, as in .rounded(0), the call outputs nothing and no error is raised.

questions.text: Which Less declaration makes the compiler output 15px?
questions.explanation: Less evaluates + at compile time. Less 4 leaves calc() untouched for the browser, so that option outputs calc(10px + 5px) rather than 15px.

questions.text: In Less 4 with the default math setting, what does width: 10px / 2; compile to?
questions.explanation: Since Less 4, division with / is only performed inside parentheses because / is also a CSS separator. Write (10px / 2) to get 5px.

questions.text: Which Bootstrap 5 class removes the horizontal gutters between columns in a row?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5's gutter utilities are .g-*, .gx-* (horizontal) and .gy-* (vertical), so .gx-0 sets horizontal gutters to zero. .no-gutters was the Bootstrap 4 class.

questions.text: Which attributes make a button open a Bootstrap 5 offcanvas panel with id="menu"?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 plugins use the data-bs-* prefix: data-bs-toggle names the component and data-bs-target selects the element. Unprefixed data-toggle is Bootstrap 4 syntax.

questions.text: In Bootstrap 5, which wrapper keeps an embedded video at a 16:9 aspect ratio?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 replaced the v4 embed-responsive helpers with .ratio plus a modifier such as .ratio-16x9. Child iframes or videos are stretched to fill the box.

questions.text: In a Bootstrap 5 Sass build, where should $primary: #ff6347; go so Bootstrap uses it?
options: Before importing Bootstrap's Sass, because its variables are declared with !default
After importing Bootstrap's Sass, so it overrides the compiled output
In a JavaScript config object passed to bootstrap.bundle.js
questions.explanation: !default assigns a value only when the variable isn't already set, so your value must exist first. Editing files in node_modules is lost on reinstall, and Sass variables can't change after compilation.

questions.text: Which Bootstrap class makes an element stick to the top of the viewport once you scroll past it?
questions.explanation: .sticky-top applies position: sticky; top: 0, so the element scrolls normally until it reaches the top and then stays there. .fixed-top is always fixed and removed from normal flow.

questions.text: In Bootstrap 5, which class makes a column 6 of 12 grid columns wide on every screen size?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 has no xs infix: unprefixed classes apply from 0px up. .col-sm-6 applies only from the sm breakpoint (576px), and .col-xs-6 was Bootstrap 3 syntax.

questions.text: Which Bootstrap 5 JavaScript file already includes Popper, so dropdowns and tooltips work without loading Popper separately?
questions.explanation: The bundle build includes Popper, which dropdowns, popovers and tooltips use for positioning. bootstrap.min.js and the ESM build expect you to load Popper yourself.

questions.text: Which JavaScript dependency did Bootstrap 5 drop compared with Bootstrap 4?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 plugins are written in plain JavaScript and no longer need jQuery. Popper is still required for positioned components, which is why the bundle build includes it.

questions.text: In Bootstrap 5.3, how do you switch a page or a single component to the built-in dark color mode?
options: Add the .dark-mode class to the element
questions.explanation: Color modes, added in 5.3, are driven by the data-bs-theme attribute, which switches Bootstrap's CSS variables. Set it on <html> for the whole page or on a component for part of it.

questions.text: In Bootstrap 5, which class creates a centered container whose max-width steps up at each breakpoint?
questions.explanation: .container sets a different max-width at each breakpoint. .container-fluid is always 100% wide, and the other two classes don't exist.

questions.text: Which class combination makes a Bootstrap column full width on small screens and half width from the md breakpoint up?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap is mobile-first: .col-12 applies from 0px, and .col-md-6 overrides it from 768px. The lg version stays full width until 992px.

questions.text: Which Bootstrap utility horizontally centers a block element that has a set width?
questions.explanation: .mx-auto sets left and right margins to auto, which splits the free space equally. .ms-auto only pushes the element to the end, and .text-center centers inline content inside it.

questions.text: In Bootstrap 5, which attribute on a button opens a modal when the button is clicked (together with data-bs-target)?
questions.explanation: data-bs-toggle="modal" with data-bs-target="#id" opens the matching modal without custom JavaScript. data-toggle without the bs prefix is the Bootstrap 4 attribute.

questions.text: Which Sass map in Bootstrap's source defines the theme colors such as primary, success and danger?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap loops over $theme-colors to generate .btn-*, .text-*, .bg-* and other variants. Adding a key to this map creates a full set of classes for a new color.

questions.text: How do you disable a <button class="btn btn-primary"> in Bootstrap?
options: Add the disabled attribute to the button
Add the .btn-disabled class to the button
Add the .inactive class to the button
questions.explanation: disabled is a boolean HTML attribute: it blocks clicks and focus, and Bootstrap styles it. The .disabled class is meant for link-styled buttons (<a class="btn">), which also need aria-disabled="true".

questions.text: Which media query matches Bootstrap 5's lg breakpoint and wider?
questions.explanation: The defaults are sm 576px, md 768px, lg 992px, xl 1200px and xxl 1400px. Bootstrap's responsive classes use min-width, so they apply from the breakpoint upward.

questions.text: In a Bootstrap 5 navbar, which class sets the breakpoint from which the menu is shown expanded instead of collapsed behind the toggler?
questions.explanation: .navbar-expand-{breakpoint} shows the links inline from that breakpoint up. Below it, the .collapse.navbar-collapse content is hidden behind a .navbar-toggler button.

questions.text: Which Bootstrap 5 utility keeps flex items on a single line instead of wrapping?
questions.explanation: .flex-nowrap sets flex-wrap: nowrap on the flex container. .text-nowrap prevents text inside an element from wrapping, which is a different property (white-space).

questions.text: What does Bootstrap's .order-md-1 class do?
options: Resets the item's order to source order
Hides the item from the md breakpoint upward
questions.explanation: Like other responsive utilities, .order-md-1 uses a min-width media query. It changes visual order only; reading and tab order still follow the DOM.

questions.text: Which Bootstrap 5 class scales an image down to fit its parent's width?
questions.explanation: .img-fluid applies max-width: 100%; height: auto;, so the image shrinks with its container without growing beyond its natural size. .img-responsive was the Bootstrap 3 name.

questions.text: How do you enable right-to-left (RTL) layout with Bootstrap 5?
options: Set dir="rtl" on <html> and keep the standard stylesheet
Set dir="rtl" on <html> and load the bootstrap.rtl.min.css build
Set lang="ar" on <html> so Bootstrap flips the layout
questions.explanation: The RTL build mirrors directional styles such as margins, floats and .ms-*/.me-*, and dir="rtl" sets the browser's text direction. Both are needed; lang alone doesn't change direction.

questions.text: Which Bootstrap helper truncates overflowing text on one line with an ellipsis?
questions.explanation: .text-truncate combines overflow: hidden, text-overflow: ellipsis and white-space: nowrap. The element must be display: block or inline-block for it to work.

questions.text: In Bootstrap 5.3, which helper sets a primary background together with a matching, contrasting text color?
questions.explanation: The .text-bg-{color} helpers set the background color and pick a readable foreground color automatically. .text-primary only changes the text color to primary.

questions.text: How do you change Bootstrap's default breakpoints in Sass?
options: Override the $breakpoints map after importing Bootstrap
Change the --bs-breakpoint-md CSS variable at runtime
Override the $grid-breakpoints map before importing Bootstrap
Pass a breakpoints option to the Bootstrap JavaScript bundle
questions.explanation: $grid-breakpoints generates every responsive class and media query at compile time. Media queries can't read CSS variables, so a runtime custom property can't move the breakpoints.

questions.text: Which element is intended for a page's or section's introductory content and navigational aids?
questions.explanation: <header> groups introductory material such as a logo, heading or navigation. <aside> holds tangential content and <footer> holds supporting information like copyright or related links.

questions.text: How should you provide a text alternative for a purely decorative image?
questions.explanation: An empty alt="" tells assistive technology to skip the image. Omitting alt makes screen readers fall back to the file name, and "image" adds noise without information.

questions.text: Which attribute pattern lets you store custom data on any HTML element?
questions.explanation: Any attribute starting with data- (for example data-user-id) is valid on any element and is exposed to scripts through element.dataset.

questions.text: What is the main semantic difference between <section> and <div>?
options: <section> is a thematic grouping, usually with a heading; <div> has no meaning
<div> is for layout only, while <section> is for styling only
questions.explanation: <section> represents a thematic part of a document and normally has its own heading. <div> is a generic container used when no semantic element fits.

questions.text: Inside <picture>, which child element lists alternative image sources?
questions.explanation: Each <source> offers a srcset with optional media or type conditions; the required <img> inside <picture> is the fallback and carries the alt text.

questions.text: You build a custom slider from <div> elements. Which ARIA role tells assistive technology what it is?
questions.explanation: slider (together with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax) describes the widget. Better still, a native <input type="range"> gets the role and keyboard support for free.

questions.text: What does the defer attribute on an external <script> do?
options: Prevents the script from running until the user interacts
Pauses HTML parsing until the script has downloaded and run
Downloads during parsing and runs after parsing completes, in document order
Runs the script as soon as it downloads, in any order
questions.explanation: Deferred scripts download in parallel and execute in order just before DOMContentLoaded. Running as soon as downloaded, in any order, describes async.

questions.text: What does HTML stand for?
questions.explanation: HTML is the HyperText Markup Language: markup that describes the structure and meaning of documents connected by hyperlinks.

questions.text: Which element embeds or references executable JavaScript?
questions.explanation: <script> contains inline code or references a file with src. <code> only marks up a fragment of computer code for display.

questions.text: How do you write a comment in HTML?
questions.explanation: HTML comments start with <!-- and end with -->. // and /* */ are JavaScript (and CSS for /* */) comment syntax.

questions.text: Which attribute gives an <a> element its destination?
questions.explanation: href holds the URL; without it an <a> is only a placeholder and is not focusable as a link. src is used by embedded resources such as images and scripts.

questions.text: Which markup correctly loads an external stylesheet?
questions.explanation: External CSS uses <link> with rel="stylesheet" in the <head>. <style> holds inline CSS and has no src attribute.

questions.text: Which element wraps the clickable <area> regions of a client-side image map?
questions.explanation: A <map name="..."> contains <area> elements and is linked to an image through the image's usemap="#name" attribute.

questions.text: How do you declare that a document is written in English?
questions.explanation: lang sets the language for screen-reader pronunciation, hyphenation and translation tools. dir controls text direction, not language.

questions.text: Which element holds supporting information such as copyright or related links for a page or section?
questions.explanation: <footer> contains information about its nearest sectioning ancestor or the page. <aside> is for tangential content and <summary> labels a <details> widget.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the <fieldset> element?
options: Groups related controls in a form, captioned by <legend>
questions.explanation: <fieldset> groups related controls such as a set of radio buttons, and its <legend> gives the group an accessible name. Disabling a fieldset disables every control inside it.

questions.text: Which <form> attribute specifies the URL that receives submitted data?
questions.explanation: action is the destination URL; method chooses GET or POST, enctype the encoding and target where the response is displayed.

questions.text: What does the placeholder attribute on an <input> do?
options: Shows hint text that disappears when the user types
Validates the input against a pattern
Sets a default value submitted with the form
questions.explanation: A placeholder is a visual hint only; it is not submitted and vanishes on input, so it must not replace a visible <label>.

questions.text: Which attribute makes a checkbox checked when the page loads?
questions.explanation: checked is a boolean attribute for checkboxes and radios. selected is the equivalent for <option> elements.

questions.text: Which element displays a scalar value within a known range, such as disk usage?
questions.explanation: <meter> shows a measurement with min, max and optional low/high/optimum. <progress> shows completion of a task and <output> shows a calculation result.

questions.text: Which element represents content that is no longer accurate or relevant, such as an old price?
questions.explanation: The HTML standard defines <s> for content that is no longer accurate or relevant. <del> records an edit removed from the document, and <strike> is obsolete.

questions.text: Which element marks text with stress emphasis that changes the meaning of a sentence?
questions.explanation: <em> conveys stress emphasis. <i> and <b> are for offset text without extra importance, and <mark> highlights relevance.

questions.text: Which element marks text as having strong importance, seriousness or urgency?
questions.explanation: <strong> represents strong importance, such as a warning. <em> is stress emphasis, and <highlight>/<important> are not HTML elements.

questions.text: What does the <base> element define?
options: The background color of the page
The base URL used to resolve relative URLs in the document
questions.explanation: <base href="https://github.com/djeada/Frontend-Notes/blob/main/quizzes/..."> in the <head> changes how every relative URL is resolved, and can also set a default link target. Only one <base> is allowed.

questions.text: A <div> acts as a custom control. Which attribute makes it reachable with the Tab key in normal document order?
questions.explanation: tabindex="0" adds the element to the tab sequence at its DOM position. -1 makes it focusable only by script, and positive values reorder tabbing in confusing ways.

questions.text: Which element provides a caption for a <figure>?
questions.explanation: <figcaption> is the first or last child of <figure>. <caption> is the table equivalent and must be the first child of <table>.

questions.text: Which attribute focuses an input automatically when the page loads?
questions.explanation: autofocus is a boolean attribute. Use it sparingly: moving focus on load can disorient screen-reader and keyboard users.

questions.text: Which element embeds inline SVG graphics directly in HTML markup?
questions.explanation: Inline <svg> creates scalable vector graphics that are part of the DOM and can be styled with CSS. <canvas> is a bitmap drawing surface controlled by script.

questions.text: Which attributes implement HTML microdata for machine-readable metadata?
questions.explanation: Microdata marks an item with itemscope/itemtype and its properties with itemprop. name/content belong to <meta>, and JSON-LD in a <script> is an alternative format.

questions.text: Which tag name can be registered as a custom element with customElements.define()?
questions.explanation: Custom element names must start with a lowercase ASCII letter, contain a hyphen and have no uppercase letters, which keeps them from clashing with built-in elements.

questions.text: What does <meta charset="UTF-8"> do?
options: Sets the encoding of the <title> only
Declares the character encoding used to decode the document's bytes
Sets the encoding used for form submissions only
questions.explanation: The charset declaration tells the browser how to turn bytes into characters. It should appear within the first 1024 bytes of the document, early in <head>.

questions.text: What does the novalidate attribute on a <form> do?
options: Disables the browser's constraint validation when the form is submitted
Removes the required attribute from all fields
questions.explanation: novalidate skips native checks such as required and type="email" on submit, often because a script shows custom errors. Server-side validation is unaffected and still needed.

questions.text: Which element represents a self-contained composition, such as a blog post or a comment?
questions.explanation: <article> is content that makes sense on its own and could be syndicated. <section> groups part of a larger whole.

questions.text: What is the role of the <template> element?
options: Holds inert markup that is not rendered until cloned by script
Marks markup that only the server processes
questions.explanation: Content inside <template> is parsed but not rendered, and its scripts and images do not run or load until a script clones template.content into the document.

questions.text: Which attribute makes <audio> or <video> start playing as soon as it can?
questions.explanation: autoplay requests automatic playback, but browsers usually block unmuted autoplay, so videos typically also need muted.

questions.text: Which input accepts only numbers from 1 to 10 using built-in validation?
questions.explanation: min and max constrain number inputs. [1-10] is a character class matching 1 or 0, and min/max have no effect on text inputs.

questions.text: Which element embeds another HTML document as a nested browsing context?
questions.explanation: <iframe> loads a full document in its own browsing context and supports sandbox, allow and loading. <embed> and <object> are generic plugin-style embeds; <include> doesn't exist.

questions.text: What do the async and defer attributes on an external classic script have in common?
options: Both execute the script before parsing continues
Both guarantee the scripts run in document order
Both download the script without blocking HTML parsing
Both delay execution until the load event
questions.explanation: Both fetch in parallel with parsing. They differ in execution: defer runs in order after parsing, while async runs as soon as the file arrives, in any order.

questions.text: Which rel value stops a link from sending the Referer header to the destination?
questions.explanation: noreferrer omits the Referer header and also implies noopener. noopener alone only stops the new page from accessing window.opener.

questions.text: What does the hidden attribute do to an element?
options: Hides it visually but keeps its space in the layout
Marks it as not currently relevant, so it isn't rendered or announced
Hides it only on small screens
Hides it visually but keeps it available to screen readers
questions.explanation: hidden acts like display: none by default, removing the element from layout and the accessibility tree. Hiding while keeping space is visibility: hidden.

questions.text: Which tag tells the browser to fetch a critical font early, before CSS discovers it?
questions.explanation: rel="preload" with the right as value fetches a resource needed for the current page at high priority; fonts also need crossorigin. prefetch is a low-priority hint for future navigations.

questions.text: Which tag creates an ordered (numbered) list?
questions.explanation: <ol> is for items where order matters, <ul> for unordered items and <dl> for term–description pairs. <li> is a list item inside <ol> or <ul>.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the <meta> element?
options: To add images to a page
To provide metadata about the document, such as encoding or viewport
To create links to other pages
To define the page's main heading
questions.explanation: <meta> lives in <head> and supplies information like charset, viewport and description that browsers and search engines read but users don't see.

questions.text: Which element embeds a video with native playback controls?
questions.explanation: <video controls> plays video natively; <source> children can offer multiple formats and <track> adds captions.

questions.text: Which <img> attribute specifies the image file to load?
questions.explanation: src is the required image URL. srcset offers optional alternatives for different resolutions, while alt is the text alternative.

questions.text: Which element inserts a line break within text?
questions.explanation: <br> is a void element for meaningful line breaks such as in addresses or poems. <hr> is a thematic break between paragraphs.

questions.text: Which tag creates a table row?
questions.explanation: <tr> contains the cells of one row: <td> for data and <th> for headers.

questions.text: Which element marks a major block of navigation links?
questions.explanation: <nav> creates a navigation landmark. Give multiple navs distinct names with aria-label, such as "Primary" and "Footer".

questions.text: Which attribute makes the browser refuse to submit a form while an input is empty?
questions.explanation: required triggers native constraint validation on submit. It is a usability aid only; the server must still validate the data.

questions.text: What does target="_blank" on a link do?
options: Opens the link in a new tab or window
Opens the link in the same tab
Opens the link in the parent frame
questions.explanation: _blank creates a new browsing context. Modern browsers apply noopener to it implicitly, and users should be told when a new tab opens. _parent targets the parent frame.

questions.text: A <button> inside a <form> has no type attribute. What happens when it is clicked?
options: Nothing, until a click handler is added
questions.explanation: A button's default type is submit. Use type="button" for buttons that only run JavaScript, so they don't submit the form accidentally.

questions.text: How is a <label> explicitly associated with an <input>?
options: The label's href points to the input
questions.explanation: for references the control's id, which gives the input an accessible name and makes clicking the label focus it. name is the key used when submitting data.

questions.text: A form has an unchecked checkbox <input type="checkbox" name="news" value="yes">. What does it contribute to the submitted data?
questions.explanation: Only checked checkboxes are submitted, as news=yes here. The server must treat a missing field as unchecked.

questions.text: Which value of the loading attribute defers an off-screen image until the user scrolls near it?
questions.explanation: loading="lazy" lets the browser postpone off-screen images and iframes. Don't lazy-load the main above-the-fold image, as that delays the largest contentful paint.

questions.text: What does console.log(typeof null) print?
questions.explanation: typeof null returns "object" because of a bug kept from the first version of JavaScript for compatibility. Test for null with value === null.

questions.text: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned?
questions.explanation: let is scoped to the nearest block and can be reassigned. var is function-scoped, and const is block-scoped but cannot be reassigned.

questions.text: Inside a regular function called as obj.method(), what does this refer to?
options: obj, the object the method was called on
questions.explanation: For regular functions, this is set by how the function is called; obj.method() binds it to obj. Arrow functions instead take this from the surrounding scope.

questions.text: Which method converts a JavaScript object into a JSON string?
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify() serializes a value to a JSON string, and JSON.parse() does the reverse.

questions.text:
In what order are the messages logged?

console.log('Start');
setTimeout(() => console.log('Timeout'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('Promise'));
console.log('End');
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first. Promise callbacks are microtasks that run as soon as the current job finishes, while the timer callback is a later task, even with a 0 delay.

questions.text: Which queue do promise .then() callbacks run from?
questions.explanation: Promise reactions are queued as microtasks, and the whole microtask queue is drained after each task before the browser handles timers or rendering.

questions.text: What does the async keyword before a function do?
options: Runs the function on a separate thread
Makes every return value a rejected promise
Makes the function return a Promise and allows await inside it
Delays the function until the call stack is empty
questions.explanation: An async function always returns a promise: returned values fulfil it and thrown errors reject it. It still runs on the same thread.

questions.text: How do you handle a rejection from an await expression inside an async function?
options: It cannot be handled; the program terminates
Read the error field of the object await returns
Wrap the await in a try { … } catch (e) { … } block
Pass an error callback as a second argument to await
questions.explanation: A rejected awaited promise throws at the await, so try/catch handles it like a synchronous error. Calling .catch() on the promise before awaiting also works.

questions.text: Which statement about Promise.race() is true?
options: It resolves with an array of all results
It rejects only if every promise rejects
It settles as soon as the first input promise settles, fulfilled or rejected
It ignores rejected promises and waits for the first fulfilment
questions.explanation: race adopts the outcome of whichever promise settles first. Waiting for the first fulfilment while ignoring rejections describes Promise.any().

questions.text: What does Promise.allSettled() fulfil with?
options: An array with the values of the fulfilled promises only
Nothing; it rejects if any input promise rejects
An array of { status, value } or { status, reason } objects, one per input
A count of fulfilled and rejected promises
questions.explanation: allSettled waits for every promise and never rejects because of an input, so you can inspect each outcome. Promise.all rejects on the first rejection.

questions.text: How can you limit fetch() concurrency to three requests at a time for a long list of URLs?
options: Use a small queue that starts three requests and starts the next whenever one finishes
Rely on the browser to run only three requests at a time
questions.explanation: Promise.all and fetch have no concurrency option, so you need a worker pool or queue (or a library such as p-limit). Browser connection limits are not a reliable throttle.

questions.text: When one promise passed to await Promise.all([...]) rejects, what happens?
options: The result array contains the error in that position
The rejection is ignored and the other values are returned
The await throws that rejection immediately; the other operations are not cancelled
The rejected promise is retried automatically
questions.explanation: Promise.all rejects with the first rejection reason without waiting for the rest. The other operations keep running; promises have no built-in cancellation.

questions.text: Which call aborts a fetch() that takes longer than 5 seconds?
questions.explanation: fetch has no timeout option; it is cancelled through an AbortSignal. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates a signal that aborts automatically after the delay.

questions.text: A search box sends a request for "ca", then for "cat". The "ca" response arrives last and overwrites the results. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Abort the obsolete request with an AbortController, or ignore responses for an old query
questions.explanation: await alone doesn't order independent requests; both can succeed in any order. Cancelling stale work, or checking that a response matches the current query, prevents outdated results.

questions.text: What is the result of [] + []?
questions.explanation: + converts both arrays to primitives; an empty array becomes the empty string, and "" + "" is "".

questions.text: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
questions.explanation: do…while checks its condition after each iteration, so the body runs once before the first check.

questions.text: Which expression creates a promise that is already rejected with an Error?
questions.explanation: Promise.reject() returns a rejected promise. Promise.resolve(new Error()) fulfils with an Error object as its value, and Promise.error does not exist.

questions.text: What can a regular function do that an arrow function cannot?
options: Be called with new as a constructor
questions.explanation: Arrow functions have no prototype, own this or arguments, so new throws a TypeError. Implicit returns are actually an arrow-function feature.

questions.text: Which statement imports the default export of ./math.js?
questions.explanation: A default import uses a name without braces. Braces import a named export, and import * needs as name.

questions.text:
What does this var loop with setTimeout log?

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
questions.explanation: var creates one function-scoped i shared by all callbacks, and the loop has finished (leaving i at 3) before any timer runs.

questions.text:
What does this let loop with setTimeout log?

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), i * 100);
}
questions.explanation: let creates a fresh binding of i for each iteration, so each callback closes over its own value.

questions.text: Which method adds elements to the beginning of an array?
questions.explanation: unshift() inserts at the start and returns the new length. shift() removes the first element and push() appends to the end.

questions.text: How do you make a single property of an object read-only?
questions.explanation: A non-writable property ignores assignments (or throws in strict mode). const only prevents rebinding the variable, and seal prevents adding or deleting properties but still allows changes.

questions.text: Which of these is not a primitive type in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The primitives are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. Objects, including arrays and functions, are reference types.

questions.text: What does await do inside an async function?
options: Converts the awaited value into a callback
Blocks the whole main thread until the promise settles
Pauses that function until the promise settles, then returns its value or throws its reason
questions.explanation: Only the async function is suspended; other code, events and rendering continue. A rejected promise makes await throw.

questions.text: Which built-in function deep-copies an object, including nested Date and Map values?
questions.explanation: structuredClone copies nested structures and many built-in types. Spread and Object.assign are shallow, and a JSON round trip turns Date into strings and drops Map contents.

questions.text: Which event fires when the HTML has been fully parsed, without waiting for images to load?
questions.explanation: DOMContentLoaded fires once parsing and deferred scripts are done. load waits for images, stylesheets and other subresources; ready is a jQuery concept.

questions.text: What is a closure in JavaScript?
options: A loop that captures all variables
A function that runs once and then deletes itself
A function together with the variables of the scope it was created in
questions.explanation: A function keeps access to variables from its defining scope even after that outer function has returned, which is how counters, private state and callbacks remember values.

questions.text: Which expression gives you the current call stack as a string?
questions.explanation: All major engines populate error.stack with a stack trace string. console.trace() prints a trace to the console but returns undefined.

questions.text: Which API schedules a callback to run just before the browser's next repaint?
questions.explanation: requestAnimationFrame runs once per frame before paint, which suits visual updates. Microtasks run as soon as the current job ends, and timers run as later tasks.

questions.text: What is a pure function?
options: A function that does not return anything
A function that returns the same output for the same inputs and has no side effects
questions.explanation: Pure functions don't read or change outside state, so they are easy to test, cache and reason about.

questions.text: Which method returns a new array containing the return value of a callback for each element?
questions.explanation: map() transforms every element into a new array of the same length. forEach() returns undefined, and filter() keeps or drops the original elements.

questions.text: What does immutability mean in functional JavaScript?
options: Data is never changed in place; updates create new values instead
Every variable is declared at the top level
Every object is deep-frozen by the engine
questions.explanation: Immutable updates return new arrays or objects (for example with spread or map) instead of mutating existing ones, which makes changes easy to detect.

questions.text: Which array method combines all elements into a single value?
questions.explanation: reduce() calls a reducer with an accumulator and each element, for example to sum numbers or group items.

questions.text: What is currying?
options: Turning a function of several arguments into a chain of functions that each take one argument
Passing an options object instead of separate arguments
questions.explanation: A curried add(a, b) becomes add(a)(b), which makes it easy to create specialized functions such as add(1).

questions.text:
What does this function composition log?

const compose = (f, g) => x => f(g(x));
const addOne = x => x + 1;
const double = x => x * 2;
console.log(compose(addOne, double)(5));
questions.explanation: compose applies the right-hand function first: double(5) is 10, then addOne(10) is 11. Applying addOne first would give 12.

questions.text: Which description fits a higher-order function?
options: A function written with arrow syntax
A function that takes a function as an argument or returns one
A function that always runs asynchronously
A function that is called only once
questions.explanation: map, filter, addEventListener and function factories are higher-order functions because they accept or return functions.

questions.text: What is partial application?
options: Calling a function with every argument it expects
Fixing some arguments of a function to produce a function that takes the rest
Caching the results of a function
questions.explanation: For example, const greetHi = greet.bind(null, 'Hi') fixes the first argument. Unlike currying, the new function may still take several arguments at once.

questions.text: What does console.log(0 == '0') print?
questions.explanation: Loose equality converts the string '0' to the number 0 before comparing, so the values are equal.

questions.text: What does console.log(0 === '0') print?
questions.explanation: Strict equality never converts types; a number and a string are always unequal.

questions.text:
What does calling foo() log?

var a = 1;
function foo() {
  console.log(a);
  var a = 2;
}
foo();
questions.explanation: The inner var a is hoisted to the top of foo and initialized to undefined, shadowing the outer a before the assignment runs.

questions.text:
What happens when a let variable is read before its declaration?

console.log(x);
let x = 5;
questions.explanation: let and const are hoisted but not initialized; reading them before the declaration is in the temporal dead zone and throws a ReferenceError.

questions.text: What does new Date('2025-13-01') produce?
questions.explanation: Month 13 is not valid in the ISO date format, so the constructor returns a Date whose time value is NaN. It does not throw; toISOString() on it would.

questions.text:
What does the last line log?

const arr = [];
arr.push(arr);
console.log(arr[0] === arr);
questions.explanation: push stores a reference to the array inside itself, creating a circular structure; JSON.stringify(arr) would throw for that reason.

questions.text: What is the result of typeof NaN?
questions.explanation: NaN is a special numeric value meaning "not a valid number", but its type is still number.

questions.text: Given const sym = Symbol('x'), which statement is true?
options: Symbol-keyed properties are skipped by for…in and Object.keys()
questions.explanation: Symbol keys are hidden from normal enumeration; use Object.getOwnPropertySymbols() to read them. Implicitly converting a symbol to a string throws a TypeError.

questions.text: What does [] == ![] evaluate to?
questions.explanation: ![] is false because arrays are truthy. Then [] == false converts both sides to numbers: "" becomes 0 and false becomes 0.

questions.text:
After copying with Object.assign, what does copy === obj log?

const obj = { a: 1 };
const copy = Object.assign({}, obj);
console.log(copy === obj);
questions.explanation: Object.assign({}, obj) copies properties into a new object, and === compares object identity, not contents.

questions.text: What does console.log({ x: 1 } === { x: 1 }) print?
questions.explanation: Each literal creates a separate object, and object comparison tests identity rather than structure. Compare specific fields or use a deep-equality helper instead.

questions.text:
What is the value of bar?

const obj = { get foo() { return 42; } };
const bar = obj.foo;
questions.explanation: Reading a getter property calls the getter, so bar receives its return value rather than the function.

questions.text:
In what order are the numbers logged?

async function run() {
  console.log(1);
  await null;
  console.log(3);
}
run();
console.log(2);
questions.explanation: An async function runs synchronously until its first await. The rest of the function resumes as a microtask after the current synchronous code logs 2.

questions.text:
What does sum(2) return?

function sum(x, y = x) {
  return x + y;
}
questions.explanation: Default parameters can refer to earlier parameters, so y defaults to x (2) and the sum is 4.

questions.text: What does void 0 evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The void operator evaluates its operand and always returns undefined.

questions.text: Which of these can be called on a line before it appears in the source?
questions.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their body. The var version is undefined early (a TypeError when called), and let and class bindings are in the temporal dead zone (a ReferenceError).

questions.text:
What happens here in non-strict code?

const o = {};
Object.defineProperty(o, 'x', { value: 1, configurable: false });
delete o.x;
questions.explanation: Non-configurable properties cannot be deleted. Sloppy mode fails silently with false; strict mode throws a TypeError instead.

questions.text:
What does this string-concatenation puzzle print?

console.log(('b' + 'a' + + 'a' + 'a').toLowerCase());
questions.explanation: + 'a' is a unary plus producing NaN, so the string is "baNaNa", and toLowerCase() turns it into "banana".

questions.text:
What does this object with keys 1 and '1' log?

const o = { 1: 'a', '1': 'b' };
console.log(Object.keys(o).length, o[1]);
questions.explanation: Plain-object keys are strings (or symbols), so the number 1 becomes '1' and the later property overwrites the earlier one. Use a Map when keys must keep their type.

questions.text: What does [1, [2, [3]]].flatMap(x => x) return?
questions.explanation: flatMap maps each element and then flattens the result by exactly one level, so the innermost array remains. Use flat(Infinity) to flatten completely.

questions.text: Which approach avoids "callback hell" in asynchronous code?
questions.explanation: Promises let each step return the next asynchronous operation, and async/await makes that chain read like sequential code with ordinary try/catch.

questions.text: What is referential transparency?
options: A function's ability to read global variables
An expression can be replaced with its value without changing the program's behavior
this always refers to the same object
questions.explanation: Calls to pure functions are referentially transparent: add(2, 3) can be replaced by 5 anywhere. Hidden state or side effects break that guarantee.

questions.text: Which built-in prevents changes to an object's existing top-level properties?
questions.explanation: A frozen object cannot have properties added, removed or changed. Freezing is shallow, so nested objects stay mutable unless frozen too.

questions.text: What is memoization?
options: Recomputing a result every time to save memory
Caching a function's results by its arguments so repeated calls are fast
Delaying a function until input stops, as in debouncing
Converting a recursive function into a loop
questions.explanation: A memoized fib(n) stores each computed value in a cache keyed by n, so it is computed once. It only suits pure functions whose output depends solely on their arguments.

questions.text: What does user?.address?.city evaluate to when user.address is undefined?
questions.explanation: Optional chaining (?.) stops and returns undefined when the value before it is null or undefined, instead of throwing.

questions.text: What does console.log(0 || 10, 0 ?? 10) print?
questions.explanation: || falls back for any falsy value, including 0. ?? falls back only for null or undefined, so 0 is kept.

questions.text: Which check reliably detects the value NaN without coercing its argument?
questions.explanation: NaN is not equal to itself, so === always fails. Global isNaN() coerces first, so isNaN('abc') is true, whereas Number.isNaN('abc') is false.

questions.text:
What happens when this code runs?

const user = { name: 'Ada' };
user.name = 'Grace';
console.log(user.name);
questions.explanation: const prevents reassigning the variable user, not changing the object it points to. user = {} would throw a TypeError.

questions.text:
What does this spread-copy example log?

const a = [1, { n: 1 }];
const b = [...a];
b[0] = 9;
b[1].n = 2;
console.log(a[0], a[1].n);
questions.explanation: Spread makes a shallow copy: the array is new, so a[0] stays 1, but both arrays share the same inner object, so the change to n is visible through a.

questions.text: What does [10, 1, 2].sort() return?
questions.explanation: Without a comparator, sort compares elements as strings, and "10" comes before "2". Use sort((x, y) => x - y) for numeric order.

questions.text: What does console.log('5' + 3, '5' - 3) print?
questions.explanation: + with a string operand concatenates, while - only works on numbers, so '5' is converted to 5.

questions.text: What is new Set([1, 1, 2, '2']).size?
questions.explanation: A Set keeps unique values using SameValueZero comparison: the duplicate 1 is dropped, but the number 2 and the string '2' are different values.

questions.text: What is a key advantage of Map over a plain object for a lookup table?
options: Keys can be any type, including objects, and keep their type
It never holds a reference to its keys
questions.explanation: Object keys are always strings or symbols, while a Map can use objects or numbers as keys and keeps insertion order. Weakly held keys describe WeakMap.

questions.text: Why might you use a WeakMap instead of a Map to attach data to DOM elements?
options: Its entries don't keep the element keys alive, so they can be garbage-collected
It copies the keys instead of referencing them
questions.explanation: A WeakMap holds its object keys weakly, so removing an element lets it be collected along with its data. The trade-off is that a WeakMap cannot be iterated.

questions.text: Which operator checks equality without type conversion?
questions.explanation: === compares type and value with no coercion. = assigns, == coerces types first, and => defines an arrow function.

questions.text: What does console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3) print?
questions.explanation: Numbers are IEEE 754 binary floats, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance or use integer cents for money.
